# Small bowel diverticular disease

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Gastroenterology > Diseases of the intestine and appendix > Small bowel diverticular disease*

[Original Article Link](/library/890O6R)

---

## Summary

<u>Small bowel diverticular disease</u> encompasses <u>small bowel diverticulosis</u> and <u>small bowel diverticulitis</u>. In <u>small bowel diverticulosis</u>, one or more <u>diverticula</u> form through the <u>small bowel</u> wall, most commonly the <u>duodenum</u>. <u>Small bowel diverticulosis</u> is more common in adults ≥ 40 years of age and is either congenital or acquired, with causes of acquired <u>small bowel diverticulosis</u> thought to include increased intraluminal pressure or intestinal <u>dyskinesia</u>. Patients are usually asymptomatic but may present with chronic, nonspecific symptoms (e.g., abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>fever</u>, <u>diarrhea</u>) and/or <u>GI bleeding</u>. Complications can be severe and include <u>small bowel diverticulitis</u>, severe hemorrhage, <u>mechanical bowel obstruction</u>, and pancreaticobiliary disorders. Diagnosis is typically based on imaging findings. Management depends on the clinical presentation. Asymptomatic patients require no treatment. Complications such as perforation, <u>abscess</u>, or severe hemorrhage often require <u>surgery</u>. <u>Small bowel diverticulitis</u> is the inflammation of one or more <u>diverticula</u> in the <u>small bowel</u> and is typically caused by diverticular obstruction. It is a complication of <u>small bowel diverticulosis</u>, most commonly <u>jejunoileal diverticulosis</u>, and usually affects older adults. Clinical features are often nonspecific (e.g., abdominal <u>pain</u>, <u>fever</u>, <u>vomiting</u>), and the differential diagnosis includes other causes of <u>acute abdomen</u>. Diagnosis is based on imaging findings (e.g., peridiverticular <u>edema</u>, diverticular wall thickening). Management depends on severity; patients with mild, uncomplicated cases are <u>treated conservatively</u> with bowel rest and <u>broad-spectrum antibiotics</u>. <u>Surgery</u> is the definitive treatment and is indicated for complications such as perforation, <u>abscess</u>, and obstruction.




This article only addresses acquired <u>small bowel</u> <u>pseudodiverticula</u>. For information on congenital <u>true diverticula</u> of the <u>small bowel</u>, see "<u>Meckel diverticulum</u>."
